chunks: I2C wire count and adding slaves. The question: How many pins/wires are needed? What if I have more slaves?
An I2C bus needs two signal wires, SDA for data and SCL for the clock, plus a shared ground and pull-up resistors. Adding another chip costs no extra wires.
It taps onto the same two lines, and the controller picks it by its address. So six sensors still cost two microcontroller pins. But it is not unlimited.
Addresses must not collide, and each chip adds capacitance (stored charge the pull-ups must fill), which slows every rise from low to high.
Think of a single bus route with many stops. Adding a stop needs no new road. Each stop has a number, and the driver calls the one they want. Two limits remain.
There are only 112 usable numbers, and two stops with the same number cause confusion. And every stop adds load, which slows the bus down.
Three slaves and the MCU share the same two signal wires. Adding a fourth sensor means tapping the same lines again, with no new MCU pin.
(The full drawing with pull-ups and ground is in "Drawing an I2C bus connection".)
SDA and SCL: the shared data wire and clock wire. Each chip needs only these two bus pins.
Pull-up resistor: one resistor per wire, shared by the whole bus, that lifts it to high ("I2C pull-ups: why and how to size"). Address: the 7-bit number that picks one chip.
There are 112 usable values. Address collision: two chips with the same address, so both answer at once.
Bus capacitance: the load from all pins, connectors and traces, measured in picofarads (pF) ("What is I2C bus capacitance").
Multiplexer: a chip that connects one of several side-branches to the main bus ("How many targets fit on an I2C bus").
For 5 devices, an I2C controller needs 2 pins. An SPI controller would need 3 plus 5 equals 8 : clock, data out and data in, plus a select wire per device. Now check the load.
Say the pins and traces add up to 89 picofarads, and the pull-up is 2. 2 kilohms. The rise time is about 0.
85 times 2200 times 89 picofarads about 166 nanoseconds, which is under the 300 nanoseconds limit for 400 kilohertz. Adding more devices pushes that number up.
That is the whole idea.
"I2C takes two wires, SDA and SCL, plus a shared ground, and one pull-up on each line for the whole bus.
More slaves go on the same two wires and are picked by their 7-bit address, so there are no extra pins.
The limits are address collisions, which you fix with address straps or an I2C mux, and the 400 picofarads bus capacitance limit, which you fix with smaller pull-ups, a slower clock, or a buffer."
